data.title: Choose the correct answer for each question.
data.description: Practise non-defining relative clauses that add extra information about already identified people, things and places.
learningPoints: Use commas around non-defining relative clauses.
Use who for people and which for things.
Do not normally use that in non-defining relative clauses.
Do not omit the relative pronoun.
Use which to refer back to a whole previous clause where appropriate.

sections.explain: Non-defining relative clauses are separated by commas because the information is additional, not identifying.

words.word: My brother, who lives in Bristol, is a teacher.
My brother who lives in Bristol is a teacher, when I have only one brother and this is extra information.
My brother, that lives in Bristol, is a teacher.

sections.explain: Use WHICH, not THAT, in a standard non-defining relative clause about a thing.

words.word: My car, which is ten years old, still runs well.
My car, that is ten years old, still runs well.
My car, which it is ten years old, still runs well.

sections.explain: WHOSE can introduce possession in a non-defining relative clause.

words.word: Sarah, whose son is at university, works with me.
Sarah, who her son is at university, works with me.
Sarah, which son is at university, works with me.

sections.explain: The relative pronoun cannot normally be omitted in a non-defining relative clause.

words.word: This book, which I bought yesterday, is excellent.
This book, I bought yesterday, is excellent.
This book, that I bought yesterday, is excellent.

sections.explain: A named person is already identified, so additional information is non-defining and takes commas.

words.word: David, who works in finance, is moving abroad.
David who works in finance is moving abroad, if there is only one David under discussion and the information is extra.
David, that works in finance, is moving abroad.

sections.explain: WHERE can add non-defining information about a place.

words.word: Paris, where I studied for a year, has changed a lot.
Paris where I studied for a year has changed a lot, with clearly non-defining information.
Paris, that I studied for a year, has changed a lot.

sections.summary: Using 'which' to refer to a whole clause.
sections.explain: WHICH can refer back to the entire previous idea.

words.word: He forgot my birthday, which annoyed me.
He forgot my birthday, that annoyed me.
He forgot my birthday, what annoyed me.

sections.summary: Using a preposition + relative pronoun in formal style.
sections.explain: A preposition can come before WHOM/WHICH in formal non-defining clauses.

words.word: Mr Lee, with whom I worked for five years, has retired.
Mr Lee, with who I worked for five years, has retired.
Mr Lee, that I worked with for five years, has retired in this formal non-defining structure.

sections.summary: Using 'which' after a proper noun thing.
sections.explain: Extra information about a unique or named thing is non-defining.

words.word: The Eiffel Tower, which was completed in 1889, attracts millions of visitors.
The Eiffel Tower that was completed in 1889 attracts millions of visitors, with the date as non-defining extra information.
The Eiffel Tower, that was completed in 1889, attracts millions of visitors.

sections.explain: Commas signal that the relative information is not needed to identify the noun.

words.word: My only sister, who lives in Leeds, is a doctor.
My only sister who lives in Leeds is a doctor, where the clause is needed to identify which only sister.
My only sister, that lives in Leeds, is a doctor.
